analysis.one_liner: Bans hiring anyone under 18 to handle tobacco plants or leaves on farms.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing, floor vote, or any further action before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend a 1938 federal labor law so that hiring a worker under 18 for direct contact with tobacco plants or dried tobacco leaves counts as illegal "oppressive child labor." Under existing rules, child labor limits are far looser in agriculture than in other industries, so minors can legally work in tobacco fields today. Senator Durbin introduced the bill with three Democratic cosponsors and 6 more Democrats joined later, but the Senate committee with jurisdiction never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Children who work on tobacco farms, including the children of migrant and seasonal farmworkers, gain protection from a hazard unique to tobacco: absorbing nicotine through the skin, which can cause nicotine poisoning, along with exposure to pesticides and long hours in hot fields. The change also covers 16- and 17-year-olds, who under current agricultural exemptions can legally perform this work.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Fair Labor Standards Act's definition of "oppressive child labor" to cover any employee under 18 with direct contact with tobacco plants or dried tobacco leaves, making such employment prohibited under federal child labor rules [S2][S3].
Closes an agriculture-specific gap: the bill removes tobacco-related agriculture from the exception that lets agricultural employers employ 16- and 17-year-olds in this work [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco growers and the tobacco farming supply chain, which would lose access to under-18 labor for tasks like harvesting and handling tobacco leaves, and might face higher labor costs or need to reorganize work to use adult crews.

drawbacks.text: The ban covers only direct contact with tobacco plants or leaves, so some farm tasks around tobacco fields would remain legal for minors; a supporter would concede it does not address child labor across agriculture generally [S3].

Growers would bear new labor costs and compliance risk in a labor-intensive crop, and enforcement falls on a federal agency with limited farm inspection capacity, so supporters would acknowledge the protection depends on whether the rule is actually enforced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is narrow but real: keeping under-18 workers out of direct contact with tobacco, a hazard agricultural exemptions currently allow. The cost falls on a small set of tobacco growers in the form of lost access to young labor. The bill is narrowly tailored rather than a sweeping rewrite of agricultural child labor rules, and its main weakness was not its design but that it never moved.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no further action on it before the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on April 16, 2015, with Senators Reed, Feinstein, and Brown, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee [S3][S5].
Nine Democratic senators cosponsored the bill [S4].
The bill's only recorded action after introduction was the committee referral; no hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action is listed before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco growers are better off because the bill never advanced; they continue to have access to under-18 labor for tobacco work under agricultural exemptions. No change in federal law means the status quo for child labor in tobacco farming is unchanged.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban under-18 employment in tobacco-related agriculture and referred remarks to the record

for.name: Nine Democratic senators
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, adding their support after introduction

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all nine cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and no senator is recorded as taking any action to move or block the bill on the floor.

industries.industry: Tobacco growers and tobacco farming operations
industries.note: The bill would have made it illegal to hire under-18 workers for direct contact with tobacco plants and leaves, removing a source of low-cost labor growers currently rely on under agricultural exemptions. The industry's interest in the status quo runs against the children the bill would have protected.

They buy leaf from farms and would face the same upstream labor cost pressure if child labor in tobacco agriculture were banned, though they are not directly regulated by the provision. Their supply chain's current cost structure depends on work the bill would have restricted.
